title: Precise genomic integration of large DNA fragments by donor-directed annealing using prime editing - Nature Biotechnology
gist: A Seoul National University team (corresponding author Sangsu Bae) developed prime assembly (PA), a double-strand-break-free gene-replacement platform that anneals complementary 3'-DNA flaps generated by prime editors, achieving up to 57.8% efficiency for multikilobase gene replacement, 28.1% for virus-free CD19 CAR-T engineering, megabase-scale programmable deletions, and disease-model corrections in HTT, ALB/F9, GSDME and SLC39A14 — with a patent already filed on the technology.

insights.claim: Prime assembly (PA) adapts prime editors to generate complementary 3'-single-stranded DNA flaps on both genomic DNA and donor DNA that anneal to each other, similar to Gibson assembly in DNA oligonucleotides, enabling programmable large-scale genomic excision and/or multikilobase donor insertion without double-strand breaks.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A DSB-free, single-step mechanism for multikilobase gene replacement is a direct challenger to HDR- and recombinase-dependent large-insertion platforms used across gene-therapy pipelines.
insights.quote: These 3′-flaps anneal to each other precisely, similar to click chemistry in small molecules or Gibson assembly in DNA oligonucleotides, and initiate strand exchange

insights.claim: Three PA variants were engineered with different tradeoffs: SF-PA (single flap, highest junctional precision), SFn-PA (single flap plus an extra nick to boost strand invasion), and DF-PA (dual flap, requires no homology arms and enables megabase-scale deletion but with somewhat lower junctional precision).
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Gives developers a menu of precision-versus-flexibility tradeoffs to pick from depending on whether the application needs a clean junction (e.g., safety-critical therapeutics) or large deletion capability.

insights.claim: PA accepts multiple donor formats — circular plasmid DNA, linear double-stranded DNA, and circular single-stranded DNA — ranging from 1.0 to 6.5 kb, without requiring PCR amplification or in vitro processing of the donor, unlike competing flap-annealing methods reported by other groups around the same time.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Simplified donor manufacturing (no PCR/in vitro processing step) is a practical manufacturing-cost advantage versus similar concurrently published flap-annealing methods.
insights.quote: our PA strategy uses circular dsDNA donors that do not require PCR amplification or in vitro processing, simplifying the workflow

insights.claim: In head-to-head tests with identical 4.3-kb payloads, PA tools achieved 32.5–50.5% integration efficiency with only 0.4–0.6% unwanted indels, versus DSB-dependent methods: HDR (4.2% efficiency, 65.4% indels), NHEJ (6.4%, 45.0%), MMEJ (9.7%, 45.4%), HMEJ (36.7%, 45.0%) and PAINT 3.0 (12.1%, 64.6%).
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: PA beats every DSB-dependent comparator on both efficiency and cleanliness simultaneously, the core value proposition needed to displace HDR/nuclease-based insertion in therapeutic development.
insights.locator: Main, comparison to other integration methods

insights.claim: The DSB-independent recombinase competitor eePASSIGE showed an almost undetectable indel rate but a 78.8% failure rate, because it mostly installed only the Bxb1 recombinase attB landing-site sequence without actually integrating the cargo payload.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A clean-looking indel rate can mask a much higher rate of failed cargo delivery — investors evaluating competing gene-insertion platforms should demand true-cargo-integration rates, not just indel-cleanliness metrics.
insights.quote: eePASSIGE mainly installed only Bxb1 recombinase-associated attB sequences without cargo integration, showing a failure rate of 78.8%

insights.claim: No PA tool showed genome-wide off-target integration exceeding 0.06% of total sequencing reads, versus the eePASSIGE recombinase approach whose single most frequent off-target site alone accounted for 4.0% of total reads.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A meaningfully cleaner genome-wide safety profile than a competing DSB-independent recombinase platform strengthens PA's case for therapeutic development where off-target integration is a key regulatory risk.

insights.claim: Best-case results included 57.8% gene-replacement efficiency with a 2.9-kb donor at the HEK4 locus (DF-PA), over 90% accuracy of integrated fragments, and precise donor incorporation confirmed by long-read sequencing in 93.7% (SF-PA), 84.3% (SFn-PA) and 77.5% (DF-PA) of donor-integrated reads.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Confirms the headline efficiency claims hold up under stringent long-read sequencing validation, not just flow cytometry, which is important for de-risking the platform for clinical translation.

insights.claim: Genetic knockdown experiments show PA efficiency depends heavily on RAD51 (homologous-recombination strand invasion), LIG3 (nick sealing) and DNA2 (5'-flap processing), and is unaffected by mismatch-repair inhibition, indicating PA operates through a RAD51-dependent, homology-directed strand-annealing mechanism.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Mapping the exact repair-pathway dependency helps predict which cell types or disease contexts (e.g., HR-deficient tumors, certain post-mitotic tissues) may respond poorly, and where PA efficiency could be further engineered.

insights.claim: PA still functions, at reduced efficiency, in G1-arrested (non-dividing) cells induced by the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib, a meaningful signal for applying the platform in post-mitotic tissue like liver or neurons where classic HDR-based editing is largely ineffective.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Partial activity in non-dividing cells widens the addressable therapeutic surface beyond proliferative cell types, relevant to in vivo liver- and CNS-directed programs.

insights.claim: PA replaced the expanded CAG-repeat exon 1 of the Huntington's disease gene HTT (16-17 repeats) with a corrected exon (10 repeats), achieving up to 57.8% replacement efficiency and reducing the repeat copy number in roughly 67-69% of sequencing reads.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A direct demonstration of trinucleotide-repeat correction at meaningful efficiency is relevant to Huntington's disease and other repeat-expansion disorders where current genetic-medicine options are limited.

insights.claim: PA inserted a functional F9 (factor IX) gene fragment into the liver-specific ALB safe-harbor locus with confirmed correct splicing, at up to 8.0% efficiency in HuH7 cells, modeling a hemophilia B gene-therapy design that piggybacks expression on the highly active albumin promoter rather than requiring an exogenous promoter.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A promoter-less, endogenous-locus integration strategy for factor IX could reduce insertional/immunogenic risk versus AAV-delivered exogenous-promoter constructs used in current hemophilia B gene therapies.

insights.claim: PA corrected a splicing-defect mutation in GSDME/DFNA5 (linked to autosomal dominant nonsyndromic hearing loss) at up to 19.0% integration efficiency, and separately bypassed a mutation hotspot in SLC39A14 (causing hypermanganesemia with dystonia) at up to 28.4% efficiency.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Demonstrates PA's applicability across neurological, hepatic and metabolic disease targets beyond a single flagship indication, broadening the platform's potential licensing surface.

insights.claim: PA enabled virus-free, plasmid/mRNA-based site-specific integration of a CD19 CAR cassette into the AAVS1 safe-harbor locus in primary human T cells at up to 28.1% efficiency, offering a non-viral alternative to lentiviral CAR-T manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A non-viral CAR-T manufacturing route addresses one of the largest cost and supply-chain bottlenecks in cell therapy (viral vector production), directly relevant to cell-therapy manufacturing economics.
insights.locator: Main, CAR integration in T cells

insights.claim: A major practical hurdle for non-viral CAR-T engineering is DNA-sensing-induced cytotoxicity from electroporating multiple plasmids into T cells; switching from standard P3 buffer to B1mix buffer suppressed the type-I interferon response (lower IFNB1/ISG15 mRNA) and let PA-edited T cells proliferate roughly 20-fold to over 10 million cells within 7 days.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: This buffer-based engineering workaround is a concrete, transferable solution to a known bottleneck across non-viral cell-therapy manufacturing more broadly.
insights.quote: B1mix significantly reduced DNA-induced type I interferon responses...T cells electroporated under these conditions exhibited viability and apoptosis levels comparable to control...and proliferated approximately 20-fold to more than 10^7 cells within 7 days

insights.claim: PA-generated CD19 CAR-T cells killed CD19-expressing Raji lymphoma cells in vitro, produced IFNγ and IL-2, and suppressed tumor growth and extended survival in a Raji xenograft mouse model.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: In vivo functional efficacy is the key proof point needed to move a non-viral CAR-T manufacturing method toward preclinical/IND-enabling development.

insights.claim: DF-PA achieved programmable megabase-scale genomic deletion-and-replacement, removing 100 kb or 1 Mb segments and replacing them with a 2.9-kb insert (2.5% and 1.9% efficiency respectively), and separately induced a targeted chromosomal translocation between chromosomes 14 and 19.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Programmable megabase deletion and controlled chromosomal translocation extend PA beyond therapeutic gene correction into a tool for engineered structural genome rearrangement, relevant to synthetic biology and disease-modeling applications.

insights.claim: In vivo proof-of-concept in mouse liver via hydrodynamic tail-vein injection achieved 4.3% (SFn-PA) and 1.1% (DF-PA) average integration efficiency in GFP-positive hepatocytes.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: An early but real in vivo delivery signal, though single-digit efficiency in a non-clinical delivery route (hydrodynamic injection) still leaves a large gap to therapeutically relevant in vivo delivery (e.g., LNP).

insights.claim: The authors position PA against a crowded field of large-fragment insertion methods — PASSIGE/eePASSIGE (needs a pre-installed recombinase landing pad), PAINT (still DSB-dependent), twinPE/GRAND editing/template-jumping PE (limited to hundreds of base pairs), Prime-Del (deletion-only, cannot replace), and CRISPR-associated transposons/bridge-RNA recombination (low efficiency in human cells) — arguing PA is the first system combining efficient, precise, simultaneous large-scale deletion and insertion in one step.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Explicit competitive positioning against essentially every named alternative large-DNA-insertion technology signals PA is being pitched as a category-defining platform, not an incremental improvement.

insights.claim: Several other research groups have reported similar flap-based donor-annealing strategies for large-fragment insertion around the same time, differing mainly in donor preparation methods (PCR-derived linear dsDNA, synthetic ssDNA, or plasmid-converted flaps).
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Flap-annealing prime editing for large insertions is becoming a competitive sub-field rather than a single-lab moat, so differentiation will likely come down to donor manufacturing simplicity and efficiency rather than the core concept.
insights.quote: Several groups have reported similar concepts (that is, flap-based strategies) for large-fragment insertion

insights.claim: The inventors (H.J., B.-D.J., Y.-W.K., H.W.I. and S. Bae) have filed a patent application covering the PA technology.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Active IP filing ahead of publication indicates the team is positioning PA for licensing or a spin-out in the gene-editing/cell-therapy space.
insights.quote: H.J., B.-D.J., Y.-W.K., H.W.I. and S.B. have filed a patent application related to this work.
